Workflow `wygkkd1po` is running in the background — 10 investigators, each fanning out to adversarial verifiers (roughly 25-35 agents total, since every finding gets independently refuted before it survives). I'll report when it lands.

While that runs, here's what the raw data already shows, so you have something concrete now:

**The headline number:** 335 fix commits vs 231 feat commits over 8 weeks. That ratio alone isn't damning — a team that finds its own bugs pre-merge looks identical in the log to a team shipping broken code. What separates those two stories is regressions, and there the signal is worse: 71 fix bodies mention "regress", 35 mention "broke", 4 mention "reintroduced".

**Concentration is severe.** `packages/server` owns 56 of the scoped fixes, more than the next four scopes combined. And the repeat-fix file list is not a random spread — `manage_operations.ts` has been touched by 19 separate fix commits, `manage_entity.ts` by 13, `manage_connections/handlers/crud.ts` by 13. Six of the top ten are gateway/connections plumbing.

**The pattern I'd bet on before the agents report back:** a large share of these fixes are the same bug found one call site at a time. Look at the titles clustered around scope — #2181 "scope platform conversation reads to the ambient org too", #2176 "scope threads to the ambient org", #2191 "gate search_memory connections on the shared visibility predicate", #2229 "surface pending approvals hidden by the ACL resource gate". That reads like org-scoping is enforced by convention at every query site rather than at one chokepoint, so each new query is a fresh chance to forget it. Same shape in the watcher→Behavior rename: #2114, #2113, #2105, #2041 are four separate commits cleaning up one incomplete migration.

Your own AGENTS.md already names this failure mode — "Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other instance and fix in one pass." The fact that the rule exists *and* the log shows the tail anyway is itself the finding worth chasing.

**Two things I'm having the agents specifically test rather than assume,** because they're the places a confident-sounding diagnosis goes wrong:

Whether the 884-test suite actually bites. High test count with a high bug rate usually means mock-heavy tests asserting the mock — and your own memory notes exactly that trap ("mocking the assumed error shape passes against the bug; 3 hits in one session").

Whether review is real. Scanning the merged PR list, a lot of substantial PRs show `0rev` — #2246 at 1289 lines across 17 files, #2247 at 182 lines, #2229 at 520 lines, all with zero recorded reviews. Meanwhile #2243 (2666 lines) got 9 and #2198 got 8. If the large-and-unreviewed set correlates with subsequent fixes on the same files, that's a much more actionable lever than anything about code structure. That correlation is being tested directly on 8 large PRs rather than asserted.

One caveat on method: I'm measuring fix *commits*, which counts pre-merge self-correction and post-merge breakage the same way. The verification phase is specifically instructed to separate those, and to refute any finding that confuses "healthy bug-finding" with "bugs escaping to prod." So expect the final list to be shorter than the ten investigators propose.

**Confidence so far:** high (90) on the raw counts — they're direct `git log` output I ran and can re-run. Low on causation until verification returns; everything in the paragraph above marked "I'd bet" is a hypothesis I deliberately handed to adversarial verifiers rather than a conclusion.

I'll surface the ranked diagnosis and the Monday-actionable remediation plan when the workflow completes.

SOURCE: repeat-fix-files | claimed: 25 -> verifier corrected: 3

ROOT CAUSE: `packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts` was written (in #1961) to stop exactly the drift described in finding 1, but it derives the tool action string from the SDK method name via a naive camelCase→snake_case transform: `const action = method.replace(/[A-Z]/g, c => `_${c.toLowerCase()}`)`. When the derived name isn't found in any tier map the guard hits `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;` and silently skips the method instead of failing. The correct mapping is sitting one file away, as a literal in the namespace source (`list: (input) => action("list_feeds", input, "list")` in `packages/server/src/sandbox/namespaces/feeds.ts:58`), but the guard never reads it. The result is a guard that looks like enforcement, passes CI green, and covers well under half of what it claims.

FIX: Two changes to `packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts`. First, replace the camelCase→snake_case guess with the real mapping: have `createActionCaller` in `packages/server/src/sandbox/namespaces/action-call.ts` register each `(namespace, method) -> actionKey` pair into an exported `SDK_ACTION_MAP`, and have the guard read that map. Second, delete the `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;` escape hatch and replace it with an explicit, enumerated allowlist of methods known not to route through a tier map — so a newly added method fails the build by default instead of being silently skipped. Then fix the three feeds drifts (align METHOD_METADATA to `admin`, matching how #1961 already aligned the other 24).

2 | Sibling call sites diverge silently: authorization scope is re-derived per route, and a fix to one sibling asserted the other was already correct — it wasn't
SOURCE: regressions | claimed: 15 -> verifier corrected: 7

ROOT CAUSE: Authorization scope resolution (which organization a request reads under) is implemented independently at each route rather than as one enforced chokepoint. `getAuthorizedAgentScope` and `getAuthorizedPlatformConversationScope` in `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts` are near-identical siblings that each re-derive the org — one ownership-first, one ambient-first. Because the divergence is invisible to the type system and to any diff-scoped reviewer, fixing one does not fix the other, and the author of the first fix explicitly (and wrongly) asserted the sibling was already correct. The same shape recurs across the codebase: `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/shared/agent-ownership.ts:14-23` carries a comment that is pure incident archaeology — 'the org id must come from the authorisation result, not from a later unscoped SELECT FROM agents WHERE id = ? The knowledge is captured as prose next to one function instead of as a structural constraint, so the next route to be written re-derives scope and re-introduces the bug.

FIX: Collapse the per-route scope derivation into one function and make bypassing it a compile error rather than an oversight. Concretely: (1) Extract a single `resolveRequestOrgScope(session, agentId)` in `routes/shared/` that implements the ambient-org-first rule plus the admin and owner fallbacks exactly once; delete `getAuthorizedAgentScope` and `getAuthorizedPlatformConversationScope` in favour of it (AGENTS.md forbids compatibility shims, so this is a straight replacement). (2) Make the DB-access layer require proof of scoping: have the query helpers accept an `OrgScope` branded value that can only be produced by `resolveRequestOrgScope`, so a route that does its own `SELECT … WHERE id = ?` cannot typecheck. (3) Add a parameterized contract test that enumerates every route in the agent-history/conversations surface from the route table and asserts each returns 404-not-leak for a per-org system agent viewed from a non-default org — one table-driven test that covers all siblings at once, rather than one bespoke test per route added after each incident. Sibling-divergence is the recurring shape here, so the test must iterate the route registry, not name routes by hand.

===============================================================================================
3 | Fix tests pin the reported instance, not the invariant — so the same bug ships again one PR later
SOURCE: test-efficacy | claimed: 60 -> verifier corrected: 70

ROOT CAUSE: Test discipline is NOT the problem: 19 of 20 recent fix commits added tests, and 9 fix commits explicitly mutation-tested them. The problem is test SHAPE. Fixes are accompanied by tests that enumerate the specific values that were reported broken, rather than asserting the invariant over the whole input domain. Because the underlying defect class is 'field X is missing from an exhaustive allowlist', an instance-scoped test passes for every field it names and stays silent for every field it does not — it can never fail for field N+1. The result is a fix that is genuinely verified red-to-green, ships, and is immediately falsified by the next field.

FIX: For allowlist/enumeration defects, require the regression test to be table-driven over the SOURCE OF TRUTH rather than over hand-listed values: iterate `Object.keys(GetContentSchema.properties)` (or the run_type constant set) and assert each key is either honored or explicitly rejected on each path, so adding a field to the schema without wiring it fails the suite automatically. Codify this in AGENTS.md's existing 'Fix the class, not the instance' rule, which currently mandates grepping for other instances but does not mandate that the TEST be class-scoped — extend it to: 'if the bug is a missing entry in an enumeration, the regression test must iterate the enumeration, not name the missing entry.' #2086's LIST_RUNS_DEFAULT_EXCLUDED_RUN_TYPES is the in-repo reference implementation.

4 | No data-access layer: every tenant-scoping and row-visibility decision is re-derived at 100+ independent SQL call sites
SOURCE: server-package | claimed: 45 -> verifier corrected: 20

ROOT CAUSE: packages/server has no repository/query layer. packages/server/src/db/ is 703 lines total (client.ts 439, migration-loader.ts 178, with-retry.ts 86) — a connection factory, retry wrapper and migration loader, and nothing else. As a result, business logic in tools/, gateway/, utils/, worker-api/ and scheduled/ hand-writes SQL directly, and each writer must independently remember to apply (a) the organization_id tenant filter, (b) the row-visibility predicate, and (c) any status/type filter. Every new call site is a fresh opportunity to forget one. Because the correctness rule lives in the author's head rather than in a type or a function, the defect is invisible to typecheck and only surfaces when a user hits the specific seam — which is why these land in prod and come back as 'fix' commits.

FIX: Introduce packages/server/src/db/repositories/ with one module per core table (runs, connections, entities, events, feeds) exposing scoped read builders that take an AuthzScope as a REQUIRED first parameter and emit the organization_id filter plus the table's visibility predicate — callers can then only express 'which rows', never 'which tenant'. Migrate the 34 runs/ readers first (smallest surface, highest recurrence). Then extend the existing scripts/check-connection-visibility-compiler.mjs pattern to a generic guard that fails CI when a raw `FROM runs|entities|events|feeds` appears outside the repository modules, with the same `-ok` escape-hatch comment convention already used at line 52 of that script.

5 | Three competing 'which org am I?' resolution strategies race in the same request, and per-org system agents make the wrong one silently plausible
SOURCE: multitenant-scope | claimed: 18 -> verifier corrected: 14

ROOT CAUSE: The codebase has three independent ways to answer 'which tenant is this request for' — the ambient org from `orgContext` AsyncLocalStorage (set by gateway middleware, membership-verified), an explicit `organizationId` argument, and org derived from OWNERSHIP (`resolveOwnership` → first `agent_users` match) — and `resolveOrgId(explicit)` at org-context.ts:29 gives the explicit argument unconditional priority (`return explicit ?? tryGetOrgId()`). The fail-open comment in `getSettings` asserts the opposite of the schema and is STILL on origin/main.

FIX: Remove the ambiguity at the type level rather than at each call site. Delete `resolveOrgId(explicit)`'s explicit-wins semantics — an ownership-derived org must never be able to override a membership-verified ambient org. Replace it with two clearly-named functions: `ambientOrgId()` (fail-closed, for request paths) and `verifiedOrgIdForToken(token)` (for worker/token paths, where the org comes from the token claim, not from ownership); make passing an org id that DISAGREES with a present ambient org throw rather than silently win. content.text:
This is the valuable part. The verification phase killed most of the intuitive diagnoses — including several I'd have handed you confidently. Let me write the synthesis directly rather than re-run the failed agent, since I now have all the material.

The verifiers established a critical control: **fix-after-fix file chaining is 58%, but feat-after-feat is 79%.** That single number reframes the whole question.

## The diagnosis

**Your bug rate is mostly not a bug rate.** Three independent verifiers converged on this and it survived every attempt to knock it down.

The 335-vs-231 ratio that looks alarming is substantially a labeling artifact. `manage_operations.ts` — the headline hot file, 19 fix commits — nets **+1453/−670 across those "fixes."** A verifier read the actual diffs: "fix(api): expose behavior IDs in operation responses" (+43/−4), "fix(operations): expose recorded initiator through list_runs." That's additive capability work wearing a `fix(` prefix. And the concentration stat that looked damning collapses against its own control: fixes chain on hot files *less* than features do. A metric that scores worse on feature work can't be evidence of defective bug-fixing.

Test discipline is genuinely strong: **83% of fix commits (288/346) touch a test file**, 19 of 20 recent fixes added tests, 9 were mutation-tested. Across 60 recent PRs: zero reverts, zero hotfixes, zero regression commits. Your AGENTS.md rules are largely *working*.

So the honest split: of 335 fix commits, roughly 200+ are healthy — self-caught pre-merge, or mislabeled features. What's left is a real and specific defect class, and it's narrower than anyone guessed.

## The one real cause: tenant identity has no canonical key

Every surviving finding is the same bug wearing different clothes. Critically, it is **not** the "someone forgot `WHERE organization_id = ?`" story — a verifier killed that explicitly, and killing it matters because it invalidates the obvious fix (RLS, a scoped query layer).

The actual mechanism: `agents_pkey` is `(organization_id, id)` (baseline.sql:2692). Agent IDs are **deliberately not globally unique** — `lobu-builder` exists under the same id in ~20 orgs. So the predicate is always present and correctly bound; the *value bound into it* comes from the wrong resolver. Three competing resolvers race in one request — ambient org from `orgContext` (membership-verified), an explicit `organizationId` argument, and ownership-derived org — and `resolveOrgId(explicit)` at org-context.ts:29 does `return explicit ?? tryGetOrgId()`, giving the explicit argument **unconditional priority over the membership-verified one**.

That's the engine behind #2176, #2181, #1783, #1848, #1346, and the #1772→#1783→#1784 chain. RLS would not have caught any of them — it would authorize the read, because the code had already resolved to the wrong tenant.

A concrete live instance, verified end-to-end: `feeds.create/update/delete` are declared `access: "write"` in method-metadata.ts:864/873/874 but sit in `OWNER_ADMIN_ACTIONS` at tool-access.ts:103-105. A member sees them in `search_sdk`, calls them, gets denied. The guard written to catch exactly this (#1961) derives action names by camelCase→snake_case, so `feeds.list` becomes `manage_feeds.list` — which exists in no tier map — and `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;` silently skips it. **The verifier ran the test: 3 passed, green, while the drift ships on main.** It checks 53 of 128 methods and silently exempts 25 including all of `feeds.*`, `authProfiles.*`, `entitySchema.*`.

## What to do

**1. Make the drift guard fail closed** — half a day, kills the whole class. In `access-model-cross-check.test.ts`, delete the `runtimeTier === null` escape hatch and replace the name-guessing with a real `SDK_ACTION_MAP` registered by `createActionCaller`. New methods then fail the build by default. Fix the three live `feeds` drifts while you're in there.

**2. Remove the resolver ambiguity at the type level** — 2-3 days, the highest-value item. Delete `resolveOrgId(explicit)`'s explicit-wins semantics; an ownership-derived org must never override a membership-verified ambient one. Split into `ambientOrgId()` (fail-closed) and `verifiedOrgIdForToken(token)`, and make a disagreeing explicit org **throw** rather than silently win. Then make `getSettings(agentId, organizationId)` require the org so the typechecker enumerates all callers in one pass.

**3. Add the two-org fixture** — 1 day. Seed the *same* agent id in two orgs with divergent config, run the full route matrix. You already wrote this ad hoc in `worker-path-org-scope-e2e.test.ts`; generalize it. This is the only test shape that catches wrong-value bugs, since single-org fixtures pass trivially.

**4. Extend "fix the class" to cover tests** — 1 hour. Your rule mandates grepping for other instances but not that the *test* be class-scoped. Add: if the bug is a missing enumeration entry, the regression test must iterate the enumeration. `LIST_RUNS_DEFAULT_EXCLUDED_RUN_TYPES` (#2086) is your in-repo reference.

What I'd **not** do: RLS, a repository layer, mandatory human review, or changing PR sizing. All were proposed and all were refuted against the actual bugs.

---

**Confidence: high (85)** on the "mostly not a bug rate" verdict and the identity-resolution cause — multiple verifiers independently reproduced the counts, and the feat-vs-fix control is decisive. **High (90)** on the feeds drift specifically: a verifier ran the test green against live broken state and traced the deny path through `enforceActionAccess`. **Medium** on the exact remediation effort estimates — nobody attempted the refactor.

One caveat I own: my earlier message leaned toward "org-scoping isn't chokepointed" and "unreviewed large PRs correlate with follow-up fixes." Both were refuted on the evidence. That's the workflow doing its job, but it's also why I'd treat the 4 survivors as the findings and not revisit the 38.

Next actions you can pick from: I can implement fix #1 (guard + three drifts) as one PR; or scope #2 by typechecking `getSettings` with a required org param to see the real caller count; or re-run the synthesis agent at valid effort if you want its independent wording; or audit how many `fix(` commits are actually features, since that mislabeling is what made this look like a crisis.

content.text:
I have enough to give you a verified verdict. The two fixes hold up very differently.

## Finding #1 (feeds drift): confirmed, and the fix is right — with one correction

Everything reproduced independently:
- **Drift is real at source.** `method-metadata.ts:864/873/874` say `access: "write"`; `tool-access.ts:103-105` put `create_feed`/`update_feed`/`delete_feed` in `OWNER_ADMIN_ACTIONS`. A member sees them in `search_sdk`, calls, gets denied.
- **Coverage numbers reproduce exactly**: 128 total / 53 checked / 50 skipped-no-tool / **25 silently skipped**. Byte-identical to the agent's claim.
- **The guard is green while the drift ships.** I ran it: `3 passed`. CI actively certifies the broken state.
- **I re-derived the drifts with a clean per-namespace parser: exactly 3, zero false positives.**

But I found something the finding got wrong, and it changes the fix. The finding proposed parsing action literals from namespace sources. **That cannot work.** `entity-schema.ts:97` computes its action at runtime — `action(payload.action as string, ...)` — so 51 of 128 methods have no statically recoverable mapping. My static parse resolved only 32.

So the fix must be **runtime registration inside `createActionCaller`**, not static parsing. That's the version the finding listed second, and it's the only one that works. The finding's proposal to "delete the escape hatch and enumerate an allowlist" is also right, but the allowlist will be ~51 entries, not the handful implied.

One more thing the finding missed: the `external` exemption is **deliberate and documented** in the guard's comments (`operations.execute`, `feeds.trigger`, `connections.test` stay write-visible while admin-enforced). Any fix must preserve it or you'll get false alarms on exactly the methods the team already reasoned about.

**Verdict: implement it, with runtime registration.** Half a day for the guard, minutes for the 3 drifts.

## Finding #2 (sibling divergence): the diagnosis is right, but the proposed fix is wrong

I nearly reported this as a false positive — `grep` found nothing in my working tree. Applying your rule and checking `origin/main` showed the file exists and I was reading stale state. Both functions are real, at lines 419 and 479.

But reading them against `origin/main` **refutes the finding's core claim.** It says one is "ownership-first" and the other "ambient-first," diverging silently. They don't. Both check `ambientOrgId` first, both carry comments explaining exactly why ("the same system-agent id exists in every organization"). They've *already been converged*. The finding's evidence — a fix asserting a sibling was correct when it wasn't — describes a past state, not current main.

The underlying mechanism is still real: `resolveOrgId(explicit)` does `return explicit ?? tryGetOrgId()`, and line 465 still feeds an ownership-derived org in as explicit. That's a genuine footgun. But it now only fires on the `!ambientOrgId` fallback path, which is much narrower than "three resolvers racing."

And the proposed fix — make a disagreeing explicit org **throw** — is actively dangerous. `resolveOrgId` has 49 call sites, including worker/token paths where the explicit org legitimately *should* win because there's no ambient context. Making disagreement throw would break those.

**Verdict: don't do fix #2 as proposed.** The narrower correct change is to make the *fallback* at line 465 not pass ownership-derived org as explicit. That's a few lines, not a 2-3 day refactor.

## Revised recommendation

1. **Guard fix + 3 feeds drifts** — half a day, verified, do it.
2. **Narrow the line-465 fallback** — an hour, not the type-level refactor.
3. **Two-org fixture** — still worth it independently; it's what would have caught the feeds drift class.

Drop the `getSettings` required-org refactor until someone re-verifies its premise against `origin/main` the way I just did here.

input.prompt:

## The verified problem

`packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts` is a drift guard that silently exempts most of the surface it claims to cover, and 3 real authorization drifts are shipping green on main right now.

I have ALREADY VERIFIED all of the following — do not re-litigate, but DO re-confirm cheaply before changing code:

1. The guard derives the tool action string from the SDK method name with a naive transform at lines 125 and 186: `const action = method.replace(/[A-Z]/g, (c) => `_${c.toLowerCase()}`)`. Real action strings do not follow this convention — `feeds.list` dispatches to `list_feeds`, NOT `manage_feeds.list`.
2. When the derived name is in no tier map, line 130 does `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;` — a silent skip instead of a failure.
3. Measured coverage: of 128 METHOD_METADATA entries, only 53 are actually checked; 50 skip on no-tool/.manage; **25 are silently skipped** (all of `feeds.*`, all `authProfiles.*`, all 12 `entitySchema.*`, and `entities.search`).
4. Three GENUINE drifts exist, which I re-derived independently with a clean per-namespace parser (exactly 3 found, zero false positives):
   - `feeds.create`: METHOD_METADATA says `access: "write"` (method-metadata.ts:864) but `create_feed` is in `OWNER_ADMIN_ACTIONS.manage_feeds` (tool-access.ts:103) → runtime tier is `admin`
   - `feeds.update`: same shape (method-metadata.ts:873 / tool-access.ts:104)
   - `feeds.delete`: same shape (method-metadata.ts:874 / tool-access.ts:105)
   The user impact: a member sees these in `search_sdk`, calls them, and hits an admin-only error.
5. I ran the guard on current main: `3 passed`. It is green while all 3 drifts ship.

## CRITICAL design constraint — a naive fix will NOT work

Do NOT fix this by statically parsing `action("...")` literals out of `packages/server/src/sandbox/namespaces/*.ts`. I tried this and it is INSUFFICIENT: `entity-schema.ts` computes its action string AT RUNTIME (see lines ~97 and ~106: `action(payload.action as string, {...}, publicMethod)`), so 51 of 128 methods have no statically recoverable mapping. A static parse resolves only ~32 methods.

The correct approach is **runtime registration**: have `createActionCaller` in `packages/server/src/sandbox/namespaces/action-call.ts` record each `(namespace, publicMethod) -> actionKey` pair it dispatches into an exported map (e.g. `SDK_ACTION_MAP`), and have the guard consult that map instead of guessing. Note `createActionCaller` already receives the namespace name as its 4th argument and the public method name as the 3rd arg to `action(...)` — the data you need is already flowing through it. Verify this yourself before building.

If after investigation you conclude runtime registration is genuinely infeasible, STOP and report why rather than shipping a static-parse fix that silently covers half the surface — that would recreate the exact bug you are fixing.

## Second constraint — preserve the deliberate `external` exemption

The guard's own comments (around lines 99-115) document that `access: "external"` is a deliberate side-effect marker, NOT a tier. `operations.execute`, `feeds.trigger`, and `connections.test` intentionally stay write-visible while their underlying actions are admin-enforced. Your fix MUST preserve this exemption or you will generate false alarms on methods the team already reasoned about. Read those comments carefully.

## What to do

1. Re-confirm the facts above cheaply (read the files, run the guard, confirm it passes green).
2. Implement runtime registration so the guard uses REAL method→action mappings.
3. Replace the `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;` silent skip with a fail-closed design: a method whose action cannot be resolved must FAIL the test, unless it is in an explicit, commented allowlist of methods known not to route through a tier map. Expect that allowlist to be sizeable — enumerate it honestly rather than making the guard lenient.
4. Fix the 3 `feeds` drifts. Align METHOD_METADATA to `admin`, which is how PR #1961 (commit e041c3479) already resolved 24 identical pairs — read that commit to match the established convention exactly.
5. MUTATION-TEST the guard, per AGENTS.md: after fixing, deliberately introduce a fake drift (e.g. flip one method's `access`) and confirm the guard FAILS. Then confirm it passes when reverted. Paste both outputs in your report. A guard that cannot be shown to bite is worthless — this is the whole point of the task.
6. Run `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts` plus any neighboring method-metadata tests.
7. Run `make pre-pr` (build, typecheck, knip, lint, naming). Then `make review-fix` on the settled diff and re-read files it changed.
8. Stage BY EXPLICIT PATH (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), commit with a conventional-commit title like `fix(server): make the SDK access-tier drift guard fail closed`. Then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list — extra files mean STOP.
9. Push and open a PR filling `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Include the mutation-test evidence (guard failing on planted drift, passing when reverted) and the before/after coverage numbers (before: 53/128 checked, 25 silently skipped).

Do NOT run `make review` — I will run that once on the settled HEAD.

## Context — read this carefully, a previous analysis of this area was PARTLY WRONG

An investigation claimed that `getAuthorizedAgentScope` and `getAuthorizedPlatformConversationScope` in `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts` are "silently diverging siblings" — one ownership-first, one ambient-first. **I checked this against `origin/main` and that claim is FALSE.** Both functions now resolve `ambientOrgId` FIRST and both carry comments explaining why ("the same system-agent id exists in every organization"). They have already been converged by prior fixes. Do not "fix" a divergence that no longer exists.

## The real, narrower issue

`resolveOrgId` in `packages/server/src/lobu/stores/org-context.ts` is:
```ts
export function resolveOrgId(explicit?: string | null): string | null {
  return explicit ?? tryGetOrgId();
}
```
An explicit argument wins UNCONDITIONALLY over the membership-verified ambient org from `orgContext` AsyncLocalStorage.

At `agent-history.ts` line ~465 (on origin/main), the ownership fallback path does:
```ts
const result = await resolveOwnership(session, agentId);
if (!result.authorized) return null;
return { agentId, organizationId: resolveOrgId(result.organizationId) ?? undefined, userId };
```
This feeds an OWNERSHIP-DERIVED org in as the explicit argument. Because `agents_pkey` is `(organization_id, id)` (see db/migrations baseline) agent ids are deliberately NOT globally unique — the built-in `lobu-builder` system agent has the SAME id across ~20 orgs. So ownership can resolve to a row in a DIFFERENT org than the request is for.

Note this path only fires when `ambientOrgId` is falsy (the earlier `if (ambientOrgId) {...}` branch returns first), so the blast radius is narrower than "three resolvers racing." Establish the true reachability yourself.

## A fix I explicitly REJECTED — do not do this

Do NOT change `resolveOrgId` to throw when an explicit org disagrees with a present ambient org. `resolveOrgId`/`requireOrgId` have ~49 call sites including worker/token paths where the explicit org legitimately SHOULD win (there is no ambient context there). Making disagreement throw would break those. I verified the call-site count but did NOT classify which are worker-token paths — part of your job is to establish that.

Trace the middleware that sets `orgContext`. If it is unreachable in practice, SAY SO and stop — do not invent a fix for a dead path. Reporting "not actually exploitable" is a fully acceptable and valuable outcome.
3. If it IS reachable, write a RED test first that demonstrates the wrong-org resolution — seed the same agent id in two orgs with divergent config and show the fallback picks the wrong tenant. Per AGENTS.md, bug fixes require red→fix→green evidence with both outputs pasted into the PR body. If you cannot reproduce it, STOP and report the dead end rather than shipping a speculative fix.
4. Then make the minimal correct fix (likely: do not pass an ownership-derived org as the explicit argument on that fallback path), and prove green.
5. Classify the ~49 `resolveOrgId`/`requireOrgId` call sites into ambient-request paths vs worker/token paths. Report the breakdown. Do NOT refactor them all — this is reconnaissance for a future decision, and scope creep here is explicitly out of bounds.
6. Run `make test-unit`. Run integration tests if you have DATABASE_URL with pgvector; if not, say so explicitly rather than claiming green.
7. Run `make pre-pr`, then `make review-fix` on the settled diff and re-read what it changed.

## Where the gap was

Every proof of #2284 up to now used a **stubbed store in a unit test**. It asserted that *given* no ambient org and a metadata row naming some org, the code declines. It never produced that state from real data — so two things stayed unproven: whether the ambiguous-row condition actually exists in a live database, and whether `findAgentOrganizations` returns the right answer when it does.

## What I closed live

Booted the server in the worktree against its own database (`lobu_feat_org_scope_fallback`), seeded the real bug condition — `lobu-builder` in **two** orgs with the same owner — and ran both queries against live Postgres:

The old org-less `getMetadata` query returned **two rows** for one agent id, with no `ORDER BY`. `rows[0]` is whichever row Postgres hands back first. That's the cross-tenant read primitive, confirmed against real data rather than a mock.

What the fix reads — `agent_users` filtered on platform + user + agent, ordered — returned **exactly one** org. So `!== 1` passes and resolves the correct tenant. On live data the fix demonstrably reads an unambiguous source where the old path read an ambiguous one.

Server came up healthy (`status: ok`, v14.6.0) running the patched code.

## What I could not close

I could not drive a real HTTP request through `/api/v1/agents/:agentId/history/threads`. This local gateway's subdomain middleware consumes the first path segment as an org slug, so every attempt returned `Organization 'v1' not found` — on both ports and with an org host header. That's a local routing artifact, not a finding about the fix. I stopped rather than reconfigure the gateway to force it.

So the end-to-end `/connect/claim` → cookie → no-ambient-org → fallback chain remains proven by **code trace plus unit test**, not by a live request. Each link I verified individually in committed source; the assembled path over HTTP, I did not.

The workflow's real payoff wasn't a process guard — it was a live bug, in the file I'd already swept and cleared.

## A real cross-tenant bug, found in code I called safe

`postgres-stores.ts:135` — the site I classified as **safe** during the class sweep, on the strength of its own comment:

> "agent IDs are globally unique and the worker token already proves authenticity, so falling back to id-only lookup is safe."

I trusted that comment. It's false, and I verified it three ways this time:

**Untruncated index dump with a row count** (the exact discipline I failed at with `connections`): `agents` has **2 indexes total** — `agents_pkey UNIQUE (organization_id, id)` and a non-unique org index. No global unique on `agents.id`.

**Empirical test**: I inserted `lobu-builder` into a second org in a transaction. **Postgres accepted it.** Two rows coexisted; I rolled back. This is the exact inverse of the slug case, where `connections_chat_slug_unique` *rejected* my insert and correctly killed that finding. Here nothing rejects it — and collisions are guaranteed by design, since `lobu-builder` and `owletto-default` are provisioned per-org.

**Consumption is unguarded**: `WHERE id = ${agentId}` with no `LIMIT`, no `ORDER BY`, then `rows[0]`. Arbitrary tenant wins.

**Corroboration from the same package**: `gateway/auth/mcp/tool-cache.ts:87` states outright that "agentId is NOT globally unique (agents PK is (organization_id, id) and ids are human slugs)" and names the consequence — org A's annotations auto-approving org B's destructive tool call. Two files in one package flatly contradict each other; `tool-cache.ts` is right.

What leaks: `models`, `guardrails`, `pre_approved_tools`, `tools_config`, `nix_config`. Another tenant's agent config and pre-approved tool policy.

An agent is on it in an isolated worktree, instructed to verify independently and stop if I'm wrong.

## The honest lesson

My class sweep cleared this site by **reading its comment**. The verification failure I asked the workflow to fix is the one that hid this bug from me — and it took the workflow to catch it. That's a sharper indictment than "sloppy queries," and it's worth stating plainly rather than burying.

## The plan itself

Of 16 proposed guards, **12 were refuted** — mostly as "prose with no failure signal." Three survivors:

1. **A PreToolUse hook** blocking schema-catalog queries piped through `head`/`tail`/`LIMIT`, with a `# TRUNCATION-OK:` escape hatch. Measured fire rate across 133 transcripts: **0.42%** (~1 per 235 Bash calls) — rare enough not to train reflexive opt-out. It fires on the *exact* command that produced my false positive. ~1h.
2. **Coverage floor on the drift guard** — assert ≥120 of 128 methods checked. (Note: it also claims 3 live `feeds` drifts, but those were fixed in merged #2283 — the workflow was reading pre-merge state. Worth flagging so it isn't re-fixed.)
3. **`// orgless-ok: <index_name>` citations** on org-less branches, CI-resolved against `pg_indexes`. `connections` earns its fallback; **`agents` has nothing to cite and fails immediately** — which is precisely the bug above.

The `scripts/absent.sh` proposal was refuted for a reason worth keeping: fed a broken pathspec it prints `ABSENT on origin/main (<sha>)` and exits 0 — it *launders a hunch into a citable artifact*. And AGENTS.md already contained the absence rule that got violated. Adding a 42nd bullet won't help.

**Confidence: 95** on the `agents` bug being real — untruncated index dump, an empirical insert Postgres accepted, and independent in-repo corroboration. **Not yet rated** on exploitability: whether real callers actually reach it without an ambient org is what the agent is tracing now, and it may come back latent-only.

I'll verify its work myself before recommending a merge.

#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook: refuse to prove a schema NEGATIVE from truncated output.
#
# Why this exists: a session queried `pg_indexes` for the unique indexes on
# `connections`, piped it through `head -6`, and the 7th row — the partial
# unique index that made the whole finding a false positive — was amputated.
# That single dropped row cost an 85-confidence wrong claim, a dispatched
# agent, and a near-miss brief authorising deletion of a load-bearing branch.
#
# The rule: truncation is fine when you are confirming something EXISTS (the
# first match proves it). It is never fine when the conclusion is "there is no
# other index/constraint/policy", because the row that refutes you is exactly
# the one that scrolls off.
#
# Scope is deliberately narrow — only the catalogs that describe CONSTRAINTS
# (pg_indexes / pg_constraint / pg_policies). information_schema is excluded:
# it is dominated by "does this column exist" checks, where `| head -1` is a
# legitimate positive test. Measured over 156,887 historical Bash calls in
# this project, this matcher fires 2 times, and both are the dangerous shape.
#
# Escape hatch (matches the repo's existing `raw-array-ok` / `squawk-ignore`
# convention): add `# TRUNCATION-OK: <reason>` to the command.

input=$(cat)
command=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')

[ -z "$command" ] && exit 0

# Explicit opt-out, with a stated reason.
echo "$command" | grep -qE '#[[:space:]]*TRUNCATION-OK:' && exit 0

# (a) Does it read a constraint-shaped catalog?
echo "$command" | grep -qE 'pg_indexes|pg_constraint|pg_policies' || exit 0

# (b) Is the result truncated? `head`/`tail` through a pipe, or a SQL LIMIT.
echo "$command" | grep -qE '\|[[:space:]]*(head|tail)([[:space:]]|$)|[Ll][Ii][Mm][Ii][Tt][[:space:]]+[0-9]' || exit 0

cat >&2 <<'MSG'
BLOCKED: truncated schema-catalog query.

You are reading pg_indexes/pg_constraint/pg_policies through `head`/`tail`/`LIMIT`.
If you are about to conclude "there is no other constraint" — the row that would
refute you is the one being cut off. This exact pattern produced a false-positive
cross-tenant bug report in this repo.

Do instead:
  - Drop the truncation and read every row.
  - Add `SELECT count(*)` alongside it so a missing row is visibly impossible.

If the truncation is genuinely safe (you are confirming something EXISTS, and the
first match settles it), say so explicitly:
  # TRUNCATION-OK: confirming the index exists, not proving absence
MSG
exit 2

## Prod query: #2287 caused no harm

`agents` lives in the **`owletto`** database (not `app`). 54 agents, 51 `agent_users` rows, 45 with owner metadata.

`support-bot` exists in **two orgs with different owners** — exactly the collision that made the pre-#2287 unscoped query dangerous. But **both have `last_used_at` NULL**, created 2026-06-02. So #2287 denied nothing anyone was using, and it closed a real collision before anyone hit it. Read-only queries only; nothing written.

## authProfiles: merged — `2df9eb5fb`

The reasoning changed once I read `handleListAuthProfiles`. This wasn't a privilege widening, as I'd framed it earlier — `list_auth_profiles` was **already** member-readable and returns `serializeAuthProfile` for *every* profile in the org, the same serializer `get` uses, with no kind filtering. Members could already read all org-shared profile metadata. The admin gate on `get` protected nothing; it just made `get` inconsistent with `list`.

So: `get_auth_profile` → `PUBLIC_READ_ACTIONS`, metadata tier → `read`. `test`/`delete`/`set_default` stay admin, `create`/`update` stay write. Verified all three on main after merge.

**Mutation-tested the guard**: planting `admin` back produced `authProfiles.get: SDK=admin runtime(manage_auth_profiles.get_auth_profile)=read` → 1 failed. Restored → 4 passed. The #2283 drift guard bites in both directions on this exact pair.

test_auth_profile     | admin    | false

I caught it by checking the source, not the output. That's the same class of trap as the truncated query, and exactly why I verify before reporting.
